title: How Biohydrocarbons Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain biohydrocarbons (hydrocarbons derived from plant matter) as a response to peak oil concerns and the inefficiency of internal combustion engines. They cover cellulosic ethanol and its costly microbe replacement and ethanol-water separation problems, camelina as a rotation crop with high yields and a reported 84.4 percent greenhouse gas savings for green jet fuel, the limits of Montana's camelina potential against US oil use, a Patagonian fungus (Gliocladium roseum) that naturally excretes diesel-like fuel and can be grown in labs, and an MIT-linked catalyst approach using heated platinum and copper to convert cellulose into hydrocarbons in fewer steps. The episode closes with listener mail from Stefano in Italy about propaganda and media control under Silvio Berlusconi, which the hosts tie back to their earlier propaganda episode.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, introduce guest producer Matt, and set up the topic of hydrocarbons as the basis of fossil fuels.

segments.title: Hydrocarbons, peak oil and engine inefficiency
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the risk of running out of oil, the debate over peak oil theory, and how internal combustion engines waste much of their energy, with unburnt hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide, ozone and soot coming out of tailpipes.

segments.title: Defining biohydrocarbons
segments.summary: Biohydrocarbons are defined as hydrocarbons derived from plant life, and the hosts note the term is roughly interchangeable with biofuels and that research is happening on many fronts.

segments.title: Cellulosic ethanol and its challenges
segments.summary: Cellulosic ethanol is made by fermenting sugars from plant cellulose and lignin using microbes and enzymes, using about 430 million tons of plant waste a year. Costs are high because microbes die and must be replaced, and ethanol mixes with water, requiring extra separation and new pipeline technology.

segments.title: Camelina as a biofuel crop
segments.summary: Camelina is grown in rotation with wheat, mainly in Montana and Idaho, yields roughly double soy, tolerates cold and drought, needs little fertilizer, and leaves a livestock feed byproduct. Green jet fuel shows an 84.4 percent greenhouse gas savings, and test flights used a fifty-fifty blend. Montana's potential is still small compared with US oil use of about 21 million barrels a day.

segments.title: Patagonian fungus that excretes diesel
segments.summary: Researchers found a Patagonian rainforest fungus, Gliocladium roseum, that grows when exposed to antibiotics and naturally excretes diesel-like fuel directly from cellulose. It can be grown in labs and also produces antibiotics as a byproduct, though the hosts raise concerns about rainforest harvesting.

segments.title: MIT catalyst research to cut steps
segments.summary: MIT researchers use heated metal catalysts such as platinum and copper to convert cellulose-derived material directly into biohydrocarbons in fewer, much faster steps. The catalyst can be reused, and the useful fuel separates on top while the bottom product can be used in plastics.

segments.title: Closing reflections on adoption
segments.summary: The hosts say people tend to rest on their laurels and that funding and a prominent advocate may be needed to push these fuels forward.

segments.title: Listener mail from Italy on propaganda
segments.summary: Stefano in Italy writes about Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi's media control, including TV ownership, newspaper shares, lawsuits against critics, and laws to ban blogs, in response to the propaganda episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to email the show and close the episode.
